thread.title_full: Richard L. Bean settles lawsuit against Knox County, officials over juvenile center resignation - NewsBreak

author: Hope McAlee
title: Richard L. Bean settles lawsuit against Knox County, officials over juvenile center resignation - NewsBreak
text:
By Hope McAlee ,
9 hours ago
KNOX COUNTY, Tenn. (WATE) — Richard L. Bean, the former superintendent of Knox County's juvenile detention center , has settled his $5 million lawsuit over his resignation from the center in 2025 after working as superintendent for decades.
In April, Bean filed a $5 million federal lawsuit against Knox County, former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs and Juvenile Court Judge Tim Irwin. The lawsuit claimed Bean was forced to resign after he said statements made by Jacobs and Irwin painted him in a bad light. Because of that, Bean said his constitutional rights were violated, and the county should be held liable for age discrimination.
According to a mediation report obtained by 6 News, all parties involved in the case met for mediation on Wednesday and reached a settlement. The details of that settlement were not listed in the report.
In May 2025 , Jacobs called out issues at the Richard L. Bean Juvenile Detention Center after he said Bean, who had been superintendent at the center since 1972, fired two employees in apparent retaliation for reporting problems at the center. The following day, Bean announced that he would be retiring, effective August 1.
An audit by the Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury released later in December revealed multiple issues with the facility, including that only one nurse had been employed, and when they were not there, security staff were responsible for administering medication to youth. Although staff assigned to that duty completed a Department of Children's Services training, there were six cases noted in the audit in which investigators found medication errors and medical deficiencies. In one case, a diabetic minor went without insulin for two weeks, and when security staff later administered the insulin, it was administered incorrectly during a night shift, the report said.
The audit also noted that there was a lack of documentation to verify if the center had been in compliance with staffing ratio requirements, and the center did not report any incidents during the 2024 or 2025 calendar years, even though they housed youth in DCS custody and were contractually required to report all incidents involving youth in DCS care.
A study conducted by the County Technical Assistance Service also described the center as "frozen in time," with outdated operating practices, record-keeping, leadership practices, and technology. The study also mentioned that a member of DCS told the assessor the facility had not met licensing requirements since 2023.
In February, the Knox County Commission voted to give control of the juvenile center to Knox County's Juvenile Court Judge. It had previously been planned for the Knox County Sheriff's Office to run the center starting in January, but the center's board of directors ultimately recommended a different course of action.
Earlier this year, another employee at the juvenile detention center filed a lawsuit also claiming age discrimination. The 68-year-old woman's lawsuit names the county and multiple other defendants at the center and claims the leadership at the center was trying to get rid of all employees who were hired during Bean's administration.

An audit by the Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury released later in December revealed multiple issues with the facility, including that only one nurse had been employed, and when they were not there, security staff were responsible for administering medication to youth.
